title: À or de? Verbs + infinitive
topic: verbs followed by à, de or nothing before an infinitive
why: Should it be commencer à or commencer de, essayer à or essayer de? This lesson sorts out which verbs take à, de or nothing before an infinitive, and shows how English -ing forms become infinitives in French. It prepares the next step: the subjunctive, for when the second verb has a different subject.

Verb + infinitive: no preposition

When a verb is followed by another verb, French puts the second one in the infinitive. Sometimes nothing comes in between, sometimes à, sometimes de. There is no logic you can deduce from English: learn each verb with its little word, the way you learn a noun with its article.

Group 1: nothing in between

You already know most of these verbs. English often has “to”, French has nothing.

verbexampleEnglish
aimer, adorer, détesterJ'aime cuisiner.I like to cook / cooking.
préférerJe préfère rester ici.I'd rather stay here.
vouloirJe veux partir.I want to leave.
pouvoirTu peux venir ?Can you come?
devoirJe dois travailler.I have to work.
savoirElle sait nager.She can swim.
espérerJ'espère vous voir bientôt.I hope to see you soon.
allerOn va dîner.We're going to have dinner.
il fautIl faut partir.We have to go.

Never add a preposition after these verbs: “j'aime de cuisiner” or “je veux de partir” are typical mistakes.

Watch venir. Je viens manger (no preposition) means “I'm coming to eat”. Je viens de manger means “I've just eaten” (unit 6). One little word changes the whole meaning!

", "

Group 2: verbs with à

A smaller group takes à before the infinitive. Many of them express an effort or a progression: starting, learning, managing, continuing.

verbexampleEnglish
commencer àIl commence à pleuvoir.It's starting to rain.
apprendre àJ'apprends à conduire.I'm learning to drive.
réussir àTu as réussi à dormir ?Did you manage to sleep?
aider quelqu'un àTu m'aides à porter la valise ?Will you help me carry the suitcase?
continuer àIls continuent à travailler.They keep on working.
penser àPense à réserver !Remember to book!
hésiter àJ'hésite à lui téléphoner.I'm hesitant to call him.

This à never contracts, since it's followed by a verb: j'apprends à écrire. And with aider, the person comes first as a direct object: J'aide ma sœur à faire ses devoirs, je l'aide à…

Penser à + infinitive is the everyday way to say “remember to” or “don't forget to”: Tu penses à acheter du pain ? (Will you remember to buy bread?).

Continuer also exists with de: ils continuent de travailler. Both are correct, with no difference in meaning. With commencer, use à.

", "

Group 3: verbs with de

The biggest group takes de (d' before a vowel). Many verbs about stopping, trying, deciding and feeling are here, as well as the expressions with avoir.

verbexampleEnglish
arrêter deJ'ai arrêté de fumer.I stopped smoking.
finir deOn a fini de manger.We've finished eating.
essayer deJ'essaie de comprendre.I'm trying to understand.
décider deNous avons décidé de partir.We decided to leave.
oublier deN'oublie pas d'appeler ta mère.Don't forget to call your mother.
accepter de / refuser deIl a refusé de répondre.He refused to answer.
avoir besoin de / envie de / peur deJ'ai envie de voyager.I feel like traveling.

The English -ing trap: after “stop”, “finish”, “enjoy”, English uses -ing. French has no -ing form: always the infinitive. “I stopped smoking” → J'ai arrêté de fumer, never “arrêté fumant”.

Asking or telling someone to do something

With demander and dire, the person takes à and the action takes de: demander à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose.

Je lui ai demandé de venir.I asked him / her to come.
Dis à Lucas de m'appeler ce soir.Tell Lucas to call me tonight.
Le médecin leur a dit de se reposer.The doctor told them to rest.

English “I asked him to come” has the same shape as “I want him to come”, but French separates them: Je lui ai demandé de venir works with an infinitive. For “I want him to come” you need a new mood, the subjunctive, in the next lesson.
